newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African rand at four-month low, but no panic.
newsitem.headline: S.African rand at four-month low, but no panic.

text.p: The South African rand moved through the key psychological barrier of 4.50 to the dollar on Monday for the first time in four months, but the panic selling many traders had feared did not appear.

Dealers said the unit had come under pressure due to worries that the relaxation of exchange controls on July 1, which will give South Africans the freedom to invest in offshore markets for the first time, might spark a flight of capital.
"I think the rand's held up well. Obviously we have given back a little back of the appreciation that we've had thus far this year," said Dave Mohr, economist at Old Mutual in Cape Town.
"But given the inflation differences between us and our major trading partners, I think it's not such a bad thing."

A jittery rand has made several mock charges at 4.50 in the past two months, prompting the setting up of stop loss orders around this level and fears that a break would send the unit spiralling toward 4.60.
In the event, the rand -- which plunged nearly 30 percent against the dollar in 1996 -- took the breach of 4.50 in its stride, helped by some support from the central Reserve Bank.
Currency dealers said importers and offshore banks had contributed to Monday's weakness as they trawled for dollars in the lead up to looser exchange controls.
But when local selling around midday took the rand to a four-month low of 4.5040 bid -- a loss of two cents on the day -- many of the dollar shorts failed to materialise.
"It was much more orderly than I thought it would be because we thought there would be a lot more stop losses," said First National Bank's chief rand trader Tony Van Dyk.
"It might have something to do with the Reserve Bank being around quoting prices. That provided the liquidity that the guys needed."
After the initial shocks, the rand settled in a narrow range either side of 4.50 for most of the afternoon.

"It's possible that some of them have pushed these stops out and it's possible that some people have taken profit earlier ahead of a possible run at these stop loss levels. That might have been some of the (dollar) demand we've seen over the last couple of weeks," said Van Dyk.
Without the stop loss pressure, the South African Reserve Bank was said to have been relatively passive in its efforts to steady the rand.
"They were active but I don't know that they had to do that much," said another dealer who asked not to be named.
Old Mutual's Mohr said Monday's slide showed the rand was shaping up as a comparatively resilient currency.

"If you look at the percentage changes on a day-to-day basis in the rand, it has been amazingly stable up to now. If you look at...major currencies you frequently see changes of one percent or more per day," he said.
Market participants said the pressure would remain on the central bank to ward off rand instability ahead of July 1.
